code.title: Compile then interpret: CPython bytecode and code objects
code.python:
import dis

source = "total = 0\nfor i in range(3):\n    total += i * 2\nprint('total =', total)"
print("source:")
print(source)

# Step 1: compile text -> code object (tokenizer, parser, AST, bytecode)
code = compile(source, "<demo>", "exec")
print("type:", type(code).__name__)
print("names used:", code.co_names)
print("constants:", code.co_consts)

# Step 2: the bytecode is a list of instructions
ops = sorted({ins.opname for ins in dis.get_instructions(code)})
print("has FOR_ITER:", "FOR_ITER" in ops)
print("has LOAD_NAME:", "LOAD_NAME" in ops)

# Step 3: the interpreter loop executes the code object
exec(code)

followUps:
The .pyc lives in a __pycache__ folder next to the source, named like mod.cpython-313.pyc, so each Python version has its own file.

The header stores the source file's modification time and size (or a hash for hash-based pycs). On import Python compares them with the real file; if they differ it recompiles and rewrites the cache. Only imported modules are cached, never the main script.

A code object is the compiled, read-only form of one function, module or class body: the bytecode plus everything it needs.

Key attributes: co_code (the instruction bytes), co_consts (literals), co_names (global and attribute names), co_varnames (locals), co_freevars/co_cellvars (closure variables), co_argcount, co_filename and co_firstlineno. A function object wraps one code object plus its globals and defaults.

Because bytecode is an internal detail of CPython, not part of the language, so Python's authors change it freely in every minor release.

Opcodes are added, removed and renumbered (3.11 added CACHE entries and removed SETUP_FINALLY; 3.12 removed more). A .pyc from 3.12 will not load on 3.13, and a tool that patches raw opcodes breaks silently. Rely on the language rules and on public APIs such as ast instead.

code.title: is versus ==, identity and caching
code.python:
class Box:
    def __init__(self, v):
        self.v = v
    def __eq__(self, other):
        return self.v == other.v      # == calls __eq__ (value check)

a = Box(5)
b = Box(5)
print("a == b:", a == b)              # True: equal values
print("a is b:", a is b)              # False: two different objects
c = a
print("a is c:", a is c)              # True: same object, two names

x = [1, 2]
y = [1, 2]
print("lists: == ", x == y, " is ", x is y)

# Small ints are cached by CPython, but that is an optimization, not a rule
n1 = int("200")
n2 = int("200")
print("200 cached (implementation detail):", n1 is n2)
n3 = int("100000")
n4 = int("100000")
print("100000 equal:", n3 == n4)

# is is right for singletons and sentinels
MISSING = object()
def get(d, k):
    v = d.get(k, MISSING)
    return "missing" if v is MISSING else v
print(get({"a": None}, "a"), get({}, "a"))

followUps:
Because == can be overridden and is cannot, so is None is always exact and fast.

A class may define __eq__ to return anything, for example a NumPy array compared to None gives an array of booleans, and a buggy class might claim to equal None. x is None compares identity of the one None object, cannot be fooled, and skips a method call. PEP 8 recommends it.

Call sys.intern when you have very many repeated strings that are compared or used as dict keys, and want one shared copy.

Example: a parser reading 10 million rows with only 50 distinct city names. Interning each name makes equal strings the same object, saving memory and making equality checks a quick pointer comparison. Do not use it for unique strings; interned strings are kept in a table and cost a lookup.

Yes: ids are only unique among objects that are alive at the same time.

Once an object is freed, CPython may reuse its memory address for a new object, so id(a) for a dead object can equal id(b) for a fresh one. Example: id([1]) == id([2]) is often True, because the first temporary list is freed before the second is made. Never store ids to track objects; keep a reference or a weakref.

code.title: Reference counting: counts rise and fall, zero frees at once
code.python:
import sys
import weakref

class Res:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
    def __del__(self):
        print("  freed", self.name)   # runs the moment the count hits 0

r = Res("A")
# getrefcount adds 1 for its own argument, so 1 name -> prints 2
print("count with one name:", sys.getrefcount(r))
box = [r]
print("count after list holds it:", sys.getrefcount(r))
alias = r
print("count after alias:", sys.getrefcount(r))

watcher = weakref.ref(r)               # weak refs do not add to the count
print("count with weakref:", sys.getrefcount(r))

print("deleting names one by one")
del alias
del box
print("  still alive:", watcher() is not None)
del r                                  # last reference: freed immediately
print("  alive after last del:", watcher() is not None)

followUps:
Because passing x to the function itself creates a temporary extra reference for the duration of the call.

If only the name x refers to an object, sys.getrefcount(x) prints 2: one for the name and one for the argument. Put it in a list and it becomes 3. Subtract one to get the count you meant. Small cached or immortal objects show huge numbers.

An immortal object has a reference count that never changes and is never freed, so it lives until the program ends.

Singletons such as None, True, small ints and interned strings are touched constantly. Immortality (3.12, PEP 683) lets increments and decrements on them be skipped, which avoids writes to shared memory. That helps copy-on-write after fork and is needed for thread-safe sharing without the GIL. Cost: a tiny check on each INCREF.

Every reference-count change writes to the object's memory page, which makes the operating system copy that page in the child process.

After fork() parent and child share pages. Reading an object in the child bumps its count, so the page becomes private and memory use grows toward double. Mitigations: call gc.freeze() before forking so the collector does not touch old objects, load data before forking, or use immortal objects and shared memory for big read-only data.

code.title: Cycles and the cyclic garbage collector
code.python:
import gc

class Node:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.other = None
    def __del__(self):
        print("  freed", self.name)

gc.disable()                      # so we control when the collector runs

a = Node("a")
b = Node("b")
a.other = b                       # a -> b
b.other = a                       # b -> a : a cycle
c = Node("c")                     # no cycle

print("deleting c (refcount alone frees it):")
del c
print("deleting a and b (cycle keeps counts at 1):")
del a, b
print("  nothing freed yet")
found = gc.collect()              # cyclic GC finds the unreachable cycle
print("gc.collect() found unreachable objects:", found >= 2)
print("garbage list empty:", gc.garbage == [])
print("thresholds are 3 ints:", len(gc.get_threshold()) == 3)
gc.enable()

followUps:
It holds objects the collector found unreachable but could not free, which in modern Python is rare.

Since PEP 442 (3.4) objects with __del__ in cycles are collected normally. Objects land in gc.garbage only if you set gc.set_debug(gc.DEBUG_SAVEALL) (all garbage is saved for inspection) or when a C type with a legacy finalizer cannot be cleared. A growing gc.garbage list is a clue, then check the referrers.

They first disabled the cyclic collector to save about 10 percent of memory, then replaced that with freezing.

With the GC on, each collection touched object headers, which dirtied copy-on-write pages in forked web workers and inflated memory. Disabling it avoided that but let cycles leak. The later fix was gc.freeze() after loading code and before forking: everything loaded so far is moved to a permanent generation that the collector ignores, so pages stay shared and new objects are still collected.

Compare what the Python-level tools see with what the process uses, then look at the cycles directly.

  1. If tracemalloc totals stay flat but RSS grows, the growth is outside Python objects (C extension or fragmentation).
  2. Run gc.collect() and note how many objects it returns; if memory drops, cycles were the holders.
  3. With gc.set_debug(gc.DEBUG_SAVEALL), inspect gc.garbage to see which objects formed the cycles.

code.title: A typed descriptor that validates on assignment

followUps:
Because cached_property stores its result by writing into the instance's __dict__, and a slotted class has no dict to write to.

The first access computes the value and saves it under the same name in obj.__dict__; later reads find it there and never call the descriptor. With __slots__ = ('a',) and no '__dict__' in it, the assignment raises TypeError. Fix: add '__dict__' to slots, or use functools.lru_cache on a method (with care) or a manual slot.

Write a class with __set__ that checks the type, as in the program above.

class Typed:
    def __init__(self, kind): self.kind = kind
    def __set_name__(self, owner, name): self.slot = '_' + name
    def __get__(self, obj, cls=None):
        return self if obj is None else getattr(obj, self.slot)
    def __set__(self, obj, v):
        if not isinstance(v, self.kind): raise TypeError(v)
        setattr(obj, self.slot, v)

Use it as age = Typed(int) in a class body.

It receives the owner class and the attribute name, and it is called once when the class body finishes and the class is created.

For class P: age = Typed(int), Python calls Typed.__set_name__(descriptor, P, 'age') right after creating P. This lets the descriptor learn its own name without you repeating it, so it can store data under '_age' or give good error messages. It only runs for descriptors present in the class body, not ones assigned later.

code.title: Attribute lookup order: data descriptor, instance dict, non-data, __getattr__
code.python:
class Data:                       # data descriptor (has __set__)
    def __get__(self, obj, cls=None):
        return "from data descriptor"
    def __set__(self, obj, v):
        pass

class NonData:                    # non-data descriptor (only __get__)
    def __get__(self, obj, cls=None):
        return "from non-data descriptor"

class C:
    d = Data()
    n = NonData()
    plain = "class value"
    def __getattr__(self, name):  # last resort, only after the normal lookup fails
        return "fallback for " + name

obj = C()
obj.__dict__["d"] = "instance d"       # try to shadow each one
obj.__dict__["n"] = "instance n"
obj.__dict__["plain"] = "instance plain"

print("d     :", obj.d)               # 1. data descriptor wins
print("n     :", obj.n)               # 2. instance dict beats non-data descriptor
print("plain :", obj.plain)           # 2. instance dict beats class value
print("other :", obj.missing)         # 3. nothing found -> __getattr__

del obj.__dict__["plain"]
print("plain after removing instance value:", obj.plain)
print("MRO:", [k.__name__ for k in C.__mro__])

followUps:
__getattribute__ runs on every attribute access; __getattr__ runs only when normal lookup has failed.

Overriding __getattr__ is safe and common for fallbacks, for example returning a default or forwarding to a wrapped object. Overriding __getattribute__ intercepts even attributes that exist, including __dict__, which is powerful but slower and easy to get wrong. Prefer __getattr__ unless you truly must control every read.

Because a property is a data descriptor, which wins over the instance dict, while a plain function is only a non-data descriptor, which loses to it.

If obj.__dict__['area'] = 5 and the class has area = property(...), then obj.area still calls the property. If instead the class has a method area, the instance dict value 5 hides it. That is why obj.method = something silently replaces a method on one object only.

Inside the hook, reach attributes through object.__getattribute__(self, name) or super().__getattribute__(name) instead of self.name.

class Logged:
    def __getattribute__(self, name):
        print('get', name)
        return super().__getattribute__(name)

Writing self.name inside would call __getattribute__ again and recurse forever. The same applies to __setattr__: use super().__setattr__ or object.__setattr__.

code.title: Plugin registry with __init_subclass__ and a tiny metaclass

followUps:
Use __init_subclass__, a hook that Python calls on the parent every time a subclass is defined.

class Plugin:
    registry = {}
    def __init_subclass__(cls, key=None, **kw):
        super().__init_subclass__(**kw)
        Plugin.registry[key or cls.__name__] = cls

Then class Csv(Plugin, key='csv'): ... registers it with no metaclass, so there is no metaclass conflict with other libraries.

type(type) returns type: the class type is an instance of itself.

Every class is an object, and objects have a class; the class of a class is its metaclass, which defaults to type. The chain would never end, so CPython ties the knot by making type its own metaclass. Example: type(int) is type, and type(type) is also type.

Either keep a registry (see above) or use type.__subclasses__(), and for iteration over the class itself add a metaclass with __iter__.

class Meta(type):
    def __iter__(cls):
        return iter(cls.__subclasses__())
class Base(metaclass=Meta): pass
class A(Base): pass
class B(Base): pass
print(list(Base))   # [A, B]

__subclasses__ returns only direct children and uses weak references, so deleted classes vanish.

code.title: Imports: sys.modules, a custom finder and a circular import
code.python:
import sys
import types

# 1. Build a fake module and see sys.modules act as the import cache
mod = types.ModuleType("foo")
mod.value = 42
sys.modules["foo"] = mod
import foo
print("foo.value:", foo.value, "same object:", foo is mod)

# 2. A custom finder on sys.meta_path serves modules from a dict
SOURCES = {"hello_mod": "greeting = 'hi from source'\nprint('  executing hello_mod')"}

class DictFinder:
    @staticmethod
    def find_spec(name, path=None, target=None):
        if name in SOURCES:
            import importlib.util
            return importlib.util.spec_from_loader(name, DictLoader())
        return None

class DictLoader:
    def create_module(self, spec):
        return None                          # default module object
    def exec_module(self, module):
        exec(SOURCES[module.__name__], module.__dict__)

sys.meta_path.insert(0, DictFinder)
import hello_mod
print("greeting:", hello_mod.greeting)
import hello_mod as again                    # cached: body does not run again
print("cached:", again is hello_mod, "in sys.modules:", "hello_mod" in sys.modules)

# 3. Circular import effect: module is in sys.modules before its code finishes
SOURCES["a_mod"] = "import b_mod\nX = 1"
SOURCES["b_mod"] = "import a_mod\nprint('  b sees X yet?', hasattr(a_mod, 'X'))"
import a_mod
print("a_mod.X:", a_mod.X)

followUps:
You write a class that provides find_spec and a loader, and add it to sys.meta_path.

The finder checks if the name is stored in the database and returns a ModuleSpec made with importlib.util.spec_from_loader(name, loader). The loader's exec_module(module) fetches the source text and runs exec(source, module.__dict__). Insert the finder first in sys.meta_path to take priority. The program above does this with a dict.

Reload re-runs the module's code in the same module object, but it does not update names that were copied elsewhere.

If another module did from foo import f, it still holds the old function after importlib.reload(foo). Existing instances keep their old class, and objects created from the old classes do not change. Submodules and the modules that imported foo are not reloaded either. Reload is fine for experiments, not for production.

Because the script directory comes first on sys.path, so your random.py is found before the standard library's.

Any library doing import random then gets your file, which lacks randint and gives errors such as AttributeError: module 'random' has no attribute 'randint'. The same happens with json.py, email.py and test.py. Rename the file and delete its __pycache__. Running with python -I ignores the script directory.

code.title: __slots__ removes the per-instance dict
code.python:
import sys

class Plain:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

class Slotted:
    __slots__ = ("x", "y")                 # fixed fields, no per-instance dict
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

p = Plain(1, 2)
s = Slotted(1, 2)
print("Plain has __dict__:", hasattr(p, "__dict__"))
print("Slotted has __dict__:", hasattr(s, "__dict__"))
print("x is a member descriptor:", type(Slotted.__dict__["x"]).__name__)

try:
    s.z = 3                                # no dynamic attributes
except AttributeError:
    print("cannot add attribute z to slotted instance")

def total_size(o):
    size = sys.getsizeof(o)
    if hasattr(o, "__dict__"):
        size += sys.getsizeof(o.__dict__)
    return size

print("slotted smaller than plain:", total_size(s) < total_size(p))

class Sub(Slotted):                        # forgot __slots__ in subclass
    pass
print("Sub instance has __dict__ again:", hasattr(Sub(1, 2), "__dict__"))
print("id is the address, stable:", id(p) == id(p))

followUps:
Compare sys.getsizeof of the instance plus its dict, or better, measure total memory for a million objects with tracemalloc.

tracemalloc.start()
items = [Plain(1, 2) for _ in range(10**6)]
print(tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()[0])

Repeat with the slotted class and subtract. Single-object getsizeof misses the dict, ints and sharing, so measure the whole collection in a fresh process.

Because a weak reference needs a slot in the object to hold the list of weakrefs, and __slots__ only gives the fields you name.

A normal class gets a hidden __weakref__ slot automatically. With __slots__ = ('x',) it does not, so weakref.ref(obj) raises TypeError: cannot create weak reference. Declare __slots__ = ('x', '__weakref__') to allow it; it costs one extra pointer per object.

The subclass gets a normal __dict__ back, so it can hold any attribute and the memory savings are partly lost.

Slots only remove the dict for classes that declare them. If Sub(Slotted) has no __slots__, instances have both the parent's slots and a new dict. Example: Sub(1, 2).z = 3 works. To keep the saving, give every class in the chain __slots__ = () or its own fields.

code.title: Specialized bytecode after warm-up
code.python:
import dis
import sys

class P:
    def __init__(self):
        self.v = 1

def read(o):
    return o.v + 1

obj = P()
for _ in range(1000):                      # warm-up so the interpreter specializes
    read(obj)

names = [i.opname for i in dis.get_instructions(read, adaptive=True)]
print("python >= 3.11:", sys.version_info >= (3, 11))
generic = [n for n in dis.get_instructions(read)]
print("plain dis ops:", [i.opname for i in generic if i.opname.startswith(("LOAD_ATTR", "BINARY_OP"))])
spec = [n for n in names if n.startswith(("LOAD_ATTR_", "BINARY_OP_"))]
print("adaptive dis shows specialized ops:", len(spec) > 0)

# Guards: changing the class invalidates the cached assumption
P.extra = 5                                 # monkey-patch after warm-up
print("still correct after patch:", read(obj))
for _ in range(1000):
    read(obj)
print("result:", read(obj))

followUps:
It is a small table of cached data stored in the bytecode right after an instruction, which the specialized instruction reads and checks.

For LOAD_ATTR the cache holds the type version and the attribute's position, so a hit skips the dictionary lookup. The cache entries sit inline in the code object's instruction array (shown as CACHE in dis(show_caches=True)), which keeps them close to the instruction for speed.

Because changing a class changes its type version tag, and every specialized instruction that guarded on the old version stops matching.

The guard fails, the interpreter falls back to the generic path and after enough misses re-specializes. Patching once at start-up is harmless. Patching inside a loop means the cache is invalidated on each pass, so you pay for deoptimization and re-warming each time. Set class attributes once, not in hot code.

Warm the function up, then disassemble it with the adaptive flag.

for _ in range(1000): f(x)
import dis
dis.dis(f, adaptive=True)

Instructions like LOAD_ATTR_INSTANCE_VALUE or BINARY_OP_ADD_INT instead of the generic names show specialization happened. If you still see plain LOAD_ATTR after warm-up, types are changing at that site. Needs 3.11 or later.

code.title: Why x += 1 needs a lock even with the GIL
code.python:
import dis
import threading

counter = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def bump_unsafe(n):
    global counter
    for _ in range(n):
        counter += 1                        # load, add, store: not atomic

def bump_safe(n):
    global counter
    for _ in range(n):
        with lock:                          # makes the compound step atomic
            counter += 1

def run(fn):
    global counter
    counter = 0
    ts = [threading.Thread(target=fn, args=(20000,)) for _ in range(4)]
    for t in ts: t.start()
    for t in ts: t.join()
    return counter

print("safe total:", run(bump_safe), "(expected 80000)")
unsafe = run(bump_unsafe)
print("unsafe total <= 80000:", unsafe <= 80000)

ops = [i.opname for i in dis.get_instructions(bump_unsafe)]
print("x += 1 on global uses LOAD_GLOBAL and STORE_GLOBAL:",
      "LOAD_GLOBAL" in ops and "STORE_GLOBAL" in ops)
print("list.append is one C call, atomic under the GIL:", [].append(1) is None)

followUps:
list.append is thread-safe under the GIL, but x += 1 is not.

A single C call such as append runs without the interpreter switching threads. x += 1 is several bytecodes (load, add, store), and a thread switch between them loses updates: two threads can both read 5 and both write 6. Use a Lock or queue for the counter. In free-threaded builds list operations use per-object locks, but compound steps still need yours.

Call sys._is_gil_enabled() (3.13 and later), which returns False when the GIL is off.

You can also inspect sysconfig.get_config_var('Py_GIL_DISABLED'), which is 1 for a free-threaded build. A free-threaded interpreter can still turn the GIL on at run time if you import an extension that has not declared support, so check the function, not just the build. Set PYTHON_GIL=0 to force it off.

Because many C extensions assume the GIL protects their data, and without it their code can corrupt memory.

An extension might keep a global buffer or update a counter without locks, which is safe only when one thread runs Python at a time. Free-threaded builds therefore expect the module to declare support (the Py_mod_gil slot). If it does not, Python re-enables the GIL when it is imported and prints a warning, so one old library does not crash the whole program.

code.title: Finding a leak with tracemalloc snapshots
code.python:
import tracemalloc
from collections import Counter

cache = {}                                  # the "leak": unbounded module-level dict

def handle(request_id):
    cache[request_id] = ("x" * 1000) + str(request_id)  # new string each time

tracemalloc.start(10)
for i in range(100):                        # warm-up traffic
    handle(i)
before = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()

for i in range(100, 1100):                  # more traffic
    handle(i)
after = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()

# Where did the growth come from? (file and line that allocated it)
top = after.compare_to(before, "lineno")[0]
frame = top.traceback[0]
print("top growth line:", frame.lineno, "in", frame.filename.split("/")[-1])
print("growth > 500 KB:", top.size_diff > 500_000)

# Who keeps it alive? Count the types held in the global dict
counts = Counter(type(v).__name__ for v in cache.values())
print("cache holds:", dict(counts))
tracemalloc.stop()

followUps:
Because the cache keeps a strong reference to every argument it has seen, including self, so instances can never be freed while the cache holds them.

The cache is stored on the function, which lives as long as the class. Each call with a new instance adds an entry, so a million short-lived objects stay in memory up to maxsize (default 128, or unlimited with maxsize=None). Fix: cache a module-level function keyed by plain values, use cached_property, or build the cache per instance in __init__.

Because Python's allocator keeps freed memory in its own arenas and the C allocator may keep pages, so the process does not always return them to the operating system.

A 256 KB arena can be released only when every block in it is free; one surviving small object pins it. Fragmentation therefore shows as high RSS with low live-object counts. Typical fixes: process long jobs in short-lived workers, use malloc_trim on Linux, or allocate large buffers separately so they are unmapped.

A weak reference points at an object without adding to its reference count, so the object is freed as soon as the real references are gone.

r = weakref.ref(obj)
r()          # the object, or None once it is freed
del obj
r()          # None

Use WeakValueDictionary for caches and WeakMethod or WeakSet for observers. The cost: you must always check for None, and not all types support weak references.

code.title: Reading closures and constants with dis

followUps:
No, a swap does not build a tuple in modern CPython: the compiler emits a direct swap of stack items.

For a, b = b, a the bytecode is roughly LOAD_FAST b, LOAD_FAST a, SWAP 2, STORE_FAST a, STORE_FAST b. Older versions used ROT_TWO and unpacking of three or more names builds a tuple. Check on your version with dis.dis('a, b = b, a'); this is an optimization, not a guarantee.

Because x += 1 compiles to separate load, add and store instructions, and the interpreter can switch threads between them.

Thread A loads 5, thread B loads 5, both add 1, both store 6: one increment is lost. Example: four threads adding 20000 each should reach 80000 but can end lower. The GIL only keeps single bytecodes atomic. Wrap the step in with lock: or use itertools.count or a queue.

It contains the nested function's code object, next to the ordinary constants of the outer function.

For def f(): def g(): return 1; return g(), f.__code__.co_consts holds a <code object g> and often None or the numbers used. The def statement runs LOAD_CONST of that code object and MAKE_FUNCTION to build the function at run time. Docstrings are also kept there as the first constant.
